The central question is whether iteratively incorporating human corrections into an uncertainty-quantifying model — say, a Bayesian neural network or an ensemble with calibrated confidence scores — systematically distorts the model's probability estimates over time, even when each individual correction is locally reasonable. The key concepts are calibration (whether a model's stated 95% confidence actually corresponds to 95% accuracy), epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty (ignorance vs. irreducible noise), human-in-the-loop feedback loops, and asymmetric feedback distributions — meaning humans don't correct randomly: they intervene more often on high-confidence errors, on outputs near decision boundaries, or on cases that are salient to them for social or cognitive reasons. An expert immediately worries that this selection bias in corrections is not missing-at-random; it's structurally correlated with the model's own uncertainty outputs, which means standard recalibration methods (temperature scaling, Platt scaling) will systematically overfit to the corrected distribution rather than the true underlying one. The subtler danger a beginner misses entirely is that the model can appear well-calibrated on held-out benchmarks while being badly miscalibrated exactly at the high-stakes decision boundaries where human correctors intervened most — a kind of Potemkin calibration that only fails when it matters most. Compounding this, asymmetric feedback tends to be self-reinforcing: a model that becomes overconfident in one region generates fewer flags there, starving future corrections of the signal needed to fix the drift.

Away from decision boundaries — in the high-confidence interior regions of input space — the model receives almost no corrective signal, so its uncertainty estimates there are updated almost entirely through the inductive pressure of the training objective and regularization, not through empirical feedback. In practice this means those regions undergo confidence inflation: the model's stated probability for dominant-class predictions drifts toward 1.0 faster than the true accuracy warrants, because the loss surface is steep toward overconfidence when no corrections push back. Ovadia et al. (2019, "Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty?") demonstrated this concretely: under distribution shift, Bayesian deep learning methods including MC-Dropout and deep ensembles maintained better calibration near uncertainty boundaries but showed calibration error climbing steeply for high-confidence predictions — and that was without any asymmetric human feedback loop accelerating the effect. The dangerous failure mode is precisely this high-confidence interior because operators and downstream systems trust those outputs most: a medical imaging classifier flagging 97% confidence on a chest X-ray read, or a fraud detection model scoring 0.02 false-positive probability on a transaction, generates no human review, no correction, and no signal — the error is invisible until it manifests as an outcome. In active learning literature this is sometimes called the "exploitation trap" — the model exploits its own confident regions, never exploring whether that confidence has drifted from reality. The asymmetry compounds because high-confidence regions often correspond to demographically or contextually homogeneous inputs: a model confidently wrong about a specific subpopulation will never receive corrections on that subpopulation if it always presents confidently, effectively creating a silent disparity.

The critical statistical property you need is that the probe distribution be covariate-unconfounded with respect to the model's own confidence scores — formally, that the probability of a sample being selected as a probe is independent of the model's output conditional on the true label, i.e., P(probe | x, y) ⊥ f(x). If probe selection is even weakly correlated with the model's confidence (e.g., you sample "easy" cases by picking inputs the model scores above 0.95), you've created a feedback loop where the probe distribution is itself a function of the miscalibrated estimator you're trying to fix — the statistical equivalent of using a bent ruler to check if your ruler is bent. What breaks specifically is consistency of the recalibration estimator: Kuleshov et al. (2018, "Accurate Uncertainties for Deep Learning Using Calibrated Regression") showed that calibration methods assume the calibration set is exchangeable with the deployment distribution; violating this produces biased temperature or isotonic regression fits that can worsen calibration in the very regions you're not probing. A concrete failure mode is shrinkage toward the probe distribution's marginal: if your probes oversample a narrow band of feature space (say, high-resolution frontal-view images in a medical system), the recalibrator learns to be well-calibrated there while the implicit regularization pressure pulls confidence estimates in unprobed regions toward the probe-set base rate, a phenomenon related to what Wen et al. (2020) called "dataset bias amplification" in active learning. In production systems like Google's medical imaging pipelines or Waymo's edge-case mining, the engineering solution is stratified importance-weighted probing — sampling with known, prespecified probabilities across input strata and reweighting corrections by the inverse probe probability — but this requires knowing your strata in advance, which is precisely what you don't know when the miscalibration is silent and regional. If you get the weights wrong by even a moderate factor, the corrected model can exhibit worse Expected Calibration Error (ECE) than the uncorrected one, because you've introduced a systematic bias with false confidence that it's been addressed.

The least model-dependent signals are input-space geometric or density-based criteria — things like distance to observed training points in a fixed embedding space, local data density estimated via kernel density estimation, or coverage metrics from the raw feature distribution — because these don't require querying the model's predictive output at all. The canonical candidate is a reference embedding from a frozen, separately-trained encoder: you probe regions that are sparse in that embedding space, using something like coreset selection (Sener & Savarese, 2018) or k-center greedy sampling, where the probe criterion is purely geometric distance from already-reviewed points. But this immediately reintroduces the problem through the back door: the frozen encoder was trained on some corpus with its own distributional assumptions, so "sparse in embedding space" really means "sparse relative to the encoder's learned metric," which encodes exactly the same biases as the data it was trained on — a frozen ImageNet encoder will call demographic subgroups geometrically "dense" if they were overrepresented in ImageNet, meaning those groups get underprobed. A more principled alternative is uniform random probing over input metadata strata — time windows, sensor IDs, geographic regions, patient demographics — where the strata are defined by variables that are causally upstream of both the model and the true label; this is what clinical trial designs call covariate-adaptive randomization, and it's the approach Rajpurkar et al. implicitly used in CheXpert validation by stratifying across hospital sites rather than model confidence. The irreducible assumption here is that your metadata strata actually partition the meaningful variation in the data-generating process — if the silent miscalibration lives within a stratum (e.g., a specific imaging protocol used at one hospital but not tracked in metadata), stratified probing is blind to it. You've traded model-circular bias for metadata-completeness bias: the probe is only as good as the causal graph you've written down, and the failures you most need to find are definitionally the ones not yet in that graph.

Failing Loudly specifically found that shift detectors operating on learned representations outperformed raw-input detectors by large margins on tabular and image data, with MMD on intermediate activations detecting shift at sample sizes roughly 3-10x smaller than output-monitoring approaches. The fundamental limit is a statistical power / detection lag tradeoff governed by the effect size of the drift: if miscalibration accumulates gradually in a low-variance subspace, the drift signal in any finite sample is indistinguishable from sampling noise until enough affected examples accumulate — and the minimum detectable effect size scales as O(1/√n), meaning slow regional drift in a rare subpopulation (say, 5% of inputs) requires quadratically more samples to detect than fast global drift. This creates a concrete danger window: in a system processing 10,000 predictions per day with 5% of inputs in the drifting subpopulation, you may need weeks of data to reach the statistical power to detect a 2% calibration shift in that region, during which the model has already made thousands of miscalibrated high-confidence predictions with no flag. The irreducible limit is that anomaly detection without ground-truth labels can only tell you the input distribution has changed, not whether the model's response to that change is wrong — you can detect that a new subpopulation has appeared, but you cannot distinguish "model handles this fine" from "model is silently wrong here" without eventually acquiring labels, which returns you to the probe design problem from the previous turn.

A concrete failure mode to avoid is alert fatigue asymmetry: Snow et al. (2008, "Cheap and Fast — But is it Good?") and subsequent crowdsourcing literature show annotator accuracy degrades non-linearly after roughly 20-30 consecutive hard cases, meaning annotators who receive drift-alert context early in a session behave differently than those who receive it late — so session position must be included as a covariate or counterbalanced across annotators. The residual problem is that even a well-specified mixed-effects bias model requires enough annotations per context condition to estimate annotator-state effects reliably, and in rare-subpopulation drift scenarios you may have only 50-100 affected cases total — too few to fit the bias model with adequate precision, meaning you face a degrees-of-freedom crisis precisely when the drift is most localized and consequential. The theoretical justification for continual learning over full retraining rests on the assumption that the data-generating process is piecewise stationary — that the drifted region represents a localized perturbation to an otherwise stable joint distribution P(x,y), so that retraining on all historical data would dilute the drift signal while fine-tuning preserves it. This assumption is formalized in the Bayesian continual learning framework (van de Ven & Tolias, 2019): if the posterior over model parameters after previous data is a good prior for the new task, sequential posterior updating is asymptotically equivalent to joint training — but this equivalence breaks when the likelihood surfaces of old and new data conflict, which is precisely what happens when the drifted region has different class boundaries than the original distribution. Full retraining is theoretically justified when drift is global and ergodic — when the new distribution eventually covers the old one and you have enough historical data to represent both — but in practice full retraining introduces calibration error through data imbalance: if the drifted subpopulation represents 5% of your combined dataset, its gradient signal is swamped by the 95% historical data, producing a model that is well-calibrated on the historical distribution and barely updated on the drift, a concrete version of the minority-class calibration failure Buda et al. (2018) quantified as requiring oversampling ratios of 10-100x to overcome in imbalanced settings. The continual learning choice introduces its own systematic calibration error through regularization mismatch: methods like EWC protect parameters important to old tasks by penalizing their movement, but "importance" is measured by the Fisher information on old data — if the drifted region requires moving exactly the parameters that were most important historically (e.g., the final-layer weights encoding the decision boundary), EWC will resist the correct update and produce a model that is miscalibrated in the drifted region specifically because it succeeded at protecting calibration elsewhere. A third failure mode specific to uncertainty-quantifying architectures is that ensemble diversity collapses differently under continual learning versus retraining: fine-tuning all ensemble members on the same drift batch drives them toward identical representations of the new region, reducing epistemic uncertainty estimates there to near zero even if the new data is genuinely ambiguous — Wen et al. (2020) showed ensemble agreement increases artifactually under sequential fine-tuning, producing exactly the overconfidence-in-new-regions failure that motivated uncertainty quantification in the first place. The honest summary is that neither choice dominates: continual learning preserves historical calibration at the cost of underfitting the drift, while full retraining risks drowning the drift signal in historical data — and the optimal choice depends on drift locality and dataset balance ratios that are empirically estimable but require held-out calibration sets from both distributions simultaneously, which are rarely available in operational settings.
